                                        PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                             §    PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                          §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                      §                  OF TEXAS


   LEAPTRAN, INC.’S RESPONSES TO COMMISSION STAFF’S QUESTIONS FOR
                              COMMENT

                                        I.         INTRODUCTION
        On January 2, 2026, the Staff (Staff) of the Public Utility Commission of Texas
(Commission) filed questions for comments on the rulemaking to implement large load
interconnection standards under Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) § 37.0561.
        Leaptran, Inc. (Leaptran) is an independent technical analytics and forecasting firm
specializing in the evaluation of electric load behavior, load ramp characteristics, and system
exposure associated with large load interconnections. Leaptran does not develop, own, operate,
or finance generation facilities, transmission facilities, distribution facilities, or large load
projects. These comments are provided solely to assist the Commission in adopting rules that
promote reliable system planning, minimize stranded infrastructure risk, and improve
transparency and predictability in the interconnection process.


                                             II.    COMMENTS
        PURA § 37.0561 directs the Commission to establish interconnection standards that
balance economic development objectives with protection against unreasonable costs and
reliability risks. Consistent with PURA §§ 37.0561 and 38.001, the Commission’s rules must
facilitate safe and reliable service while minimizing the risk of stranded or misallocated
infrastructure investments.
        In practice, this balance is most affected by uncertainty in the timing, magnitude, and
durability of large load realization. While nameplate capacity thresholds provide a useful
screening tool, the operational and financial risks associated with large loads are driven primarily
by how and when load materializes, rather than by aggregate megawatt levels alone.
Accordingly, the Commission’s rules should recognize ramp behavior as a central planning
consideration.
                                                                                          Page 2 of 5


A. Load Ramp Schedules as Planning-Critical Information
       Leaptran supports Commission rules that treat load ramp schedules as material planning
inputs, rather than solely as contractual representations. Large load projects of comparable size
may impose materially different system impacts depending on:
   •   the pace of load realization,
   •   whether load increases occur incrementally or as step changes, and
   •   coincidence with constrained or peak system conditions.
Rules that permit or encourage evaluation of load on a time-phased basis better align
interconnection decisions with actual system risk and promote consistency between
interconnection assumptions and long-term planning models.


B. Screening and Study Processes Should Address Ramp-Related Exposure
       Initial screening and subsequent interconnection studies are most effective when they
evaluate not only steady-state feasibility, but also incremental system exposure associated with
ramp timing uncertainty. The Commission should allow screening and study processes to
consider alternative ramp realization scenarios, sensitivity to accelerated or delayed ramps, and
conditions under which ramp deviations materially affect reliability or infrastructure utilization.
Such considerations may be addressed through protocols, guides, or engineering practices,
without requiring prescriptive definitions in Commission rules.


B-1. Ramp Timing and System-Level Constraint Interaction in a Coordinated Study
Environment
       As coordinated study processes evaluate multiple large loads within the same planning
cycle, transmission constraints are increasingly assessed under multi-contingency, system-wide
conditions. In this context, the system impacts of any individual load are influenced by the
relative timing and geographic clustering of other projects evaluated concurrently. Transmission
upgrades identified through contingency-based planning frequently resolve constraints shaped by
interacting load additions and evolving system conditions. The magnitude and timing of those
constraints may change depending on sequencing of ramp schedules among projects, proximity
of new loads within constrained corridors, concurrent generation development, and seasonal or
peak alignment of energization milestones.
                                                                                           Page 3 of 5


       Direct-assigned facilities required solely to physically interconnect a specific load can
typically be identified early in the process. Broader network upgrades, however, reflect system-
level interactions that mature as study assumptions are refined. Ramp-aware evaluation
frameworks improve planning transparency by characterizing how alternative ramp profiles
influence the timing and severity of modeled constraints. Such evaluation does not attempt to
attribute “use” of shared transmission facilities to individual loads. Rather, it enhances
understanding of how ramp timing affects aggregate system exposure under contingency
conditions, consistent with established cost allocation principles.


C. Alignment of Financial Security with Ramp-Driven Risk
       Financial security and commitment mechanisms serve to protect customers and the
system from risks associated with non-realization or delayed realization of large load projects.
From a system planning perspective, these risks arise when infrastructure is constructed in
anticipation of load that does not materialize as represented or when load realization materially
deviates from the ramp assumptions used to justify infrastructure sequencing. Leaptran supports
rulemaking that allows financial security requirements and release conditions to reflect
demonstrated progress toward load realization and attainment of ramp milestones following
energization. Such alignment improves risk signaling while preserving flexibility for legitimate
project development. Such alignment improves risk signaling while preserving flexibility for
legitimate project development.
       Financial security mechanisms are most effective when they reflect reasonably
anticipated exposure rather than serving as static entry barriers. In coordinated study
environments where constraint identification and transmission solutions depend on ramp
sequencing across multiple loads, security calibration may reasonably consider the credibility of
declared ramp milestones and the extent to which early energization assumptions influenced
planning outcomes. A time-differentiated or ramp-indexed security structure can discourage
unrealistic front-loaded ramp schedules that may distort planning assumptions while maintaining
appropriate flexibility for legitimate projects.
       Aligning security with ramp credibility does not require expansion of project-specific
responsibility for shared network upgrades, strengthens discipline in interconnection
representations, and improves planning realism.
                                                                                          Page 4 of 5



D. Importance of Objective and Consistent Evaluation Frameworks
       To ensure transparency and non-discriminatory treatment, differences in interconnection
treatment among large load customers should be traceable to measurable differences in system
impact or risk, rather than subjective judgment. The Commission should support the use of
objective, auditable analytical approaches that are applied consistently across projects, output
reproducible results given same inputs, and create a defensible planning record for subsequent
infrastructure approvals and cost recovery proceedings. In coordinated study environments, small
differences in ramp timing can materially affect modeled constraint outcomes. Analytical tools
that quantify ramp sensitivity under multiple contingency scenarios can improve consistency
without dictating policy outcomes or altering established cost allocation structures.


E. Relationship Between Interconnection Commitments and Load Forecasting
       Interconnection commitments established under PURA § 37.0561 will inform future
system forecasts. Forecast accuracy improves when load additions are represented as time-
phased trajectories that reflect uncertainty, rather than as binary outcomes. Leaptran believes
consideration of how interconnection standards may support improved alignment between
committed load and planning forecasts and orderly adjustment of forecasts as project status and
ramp credibility evolve. The Commission’s implementation of PURA § 37.0561 will operate
alongside evolving coordinated study methodologies. Rules that encourage realistic ramp
disclosure, iterative modeling refinement, and objective exposure analysis will enhance system-
level planning accuracy.


                                       III.    CONCLUSION
       The effective implementation of PURA § 37.0561 depends on recognizing that load ramp
uncertainty is a primary driver of reliability and stranded-cost risk associated with large load
interconnections. By encouraging time-phased evaluation, objective screening practices, and
risk-aligned commitments without prescribing specific technologies or market outcomes, the
Commission can advance economic development while protecting system reliability and
ratepayers.
       Leaptran appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments.
                                                       Page 5 of 5
